Most people have heard of the Trolley Problem:

There is a runaway trolley barreling down the railway tracks. Ahead, on the tracks, there are five people tied up and unable to move. The trolley is headed straight for them. You are standing some distance off in the train yard, next to a lever. If you pull this lever, the trolley will switch to a different set of tracks. However, you notice that there is one person on the side track. You have two options: (1) Do nothing, and the trolley kills the five people on the main track. (2) Pull the lever, diverting the trolley onto the side track where it will kill one person. Which is the most ethical choice?

My question is (ethics aside), is there any legal precendent for a situation like this, and what could be the legal consequences of each choice? If I switch the tracks, am I guilty of murder? Manslaughter? If I don't, am I guilty of five counts of negligent homicide?
Lawyers of Voat: Question about the Trolley Problem

The legal consequences are this, as I see them:

If you do absolutely nothing, there is nothing that can be done to you legally. You have no legal obligation to help anyone in such a circumstance unless you are in some kind of existing relationship that would require you to help them. There are a few such relationships recognized by law, but your hypo doesn't suggest any of those relationships. Also, if you put the circumstances into motion (e.g. you actually started the trolley rolling) then you have a duty to the people.

If you decide to 'help' and switch the lever, it's not likely that you will be held criminally liable for the resulting death of the one person. People were going to die either way, the question, in my opinion, is, did your action decrease the amount of deaths (i.e. without your actions, would there have been MORE deaths). I can't see a judge or jury considering that your actions to be criminal in that sense. You certainly wouldn't be guilty of murder or manslaughter. There are circumstances in which you try to aid someone and you end up causing harm to them or someone else, that can be considered a tort. But that would obviously be a civil lawsuit brought by the family of the one person.

You certainly wouldn't be guilty of murder or manslaughter.

I won't pretend to know the laws in all jurisdictions, but this is far from clear to me. If you move the track, you have affirmatively decided to kill the one person. It is very possible you could be guilty of murder. You are not responsible for anyone's death if you do not act. You are directly responsible for someone's death if you do.

Common law states that the Average Joe just minding his own business is under no legal obligation to provide assistance to another who is in need of assistance even in cases where the death of the person in distress is possible. That's the commonly accepted legal standard. Common law also states that once you begin to help a person in distress you are now responsible for the outcome. Obviously, that isn't always a fair determination, which is why a number of jurisdictions have a Good Samaritan law that provides a defense. However, not every jurisdiction has a Good Samaritan law, so keep that in mind.

Now, that does not speak to the moral or ethical side of the equation. I don't know if there is a moral or ethical "right" answer to the scenario. At first glance, it seems saving 5 people at the expense of 1 might seem more ethical. But, one could just as easily see the other side of that coin if the one person was someone important or there was some other factor to consider about that person (i.e. it was a child). I think the ethics question can really only be answered by your own introspection. Most likely, the answer is going to be different for different people for lots of different reasons.

In the Trolley scenario, the best legal (although not necessarily moral) choice for you is to do nothing. The second you take an action, one way or the other, you are now going to have to defend why you made your choice. As an attorney, although I am not a Prosecutor, I would like to think that the Prosecutor would not charge you at all because it's a really crappy result regardless of your choice. I would like to think that having to live with having made a choice like that is more punishment than the legal system could ever produce. However, I also know that not all Prosecutors think like I do. So yes, you could be looking at charges for your choice.

The other real problem you would face from making a choice is you open yourself up to a civil suit by the person(s) or family of the person(s) who were injured.

How would this apply in the few places (even in America) were you there is a duty to rescue?

In the United States, as of 2009 ten states had laws on the books requiring that people at least notify law enforcement of and/or seek aid for strangers in peril under certain conditions: California, Florida, Hawaii, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Ohio, Rhode Island, Vermont, Washington, and Wisconsin.

If one is in a jurisdiction where a duty to assist exists, then obviously that law would apply. I have not looked up the statutes from one of those jurisdictions, but I would have to imagine that if the law creates a duty to assist it also creates an affirmative defense from prosecution for having fulfilled that duty. In other words, you have to act, by law, but the law that requires you to act also protects you from prosecution for having acted.

In the scenario of the Trolley, I would imagine the law would also give at least a partial defense to a tort claim from the affected person or family as long as you can articulate a reasonable answer for the decision you made. I mean common sense should tell us that if the law is going to require you to act, then it should at least provide some shielding from the consequences of your action as long as your action was reasonable. The Trolley scenario is really one of those things that points out the fact that laws do not always adequately cover all the possibilities.
